stages.name: Labour supply diagram
stages.title: Labour supply diagram
stages.sub: After this, the student can draw a market labour supply curve on a diagram.

steps.q: A care home offers £9 an hour and struggles to find carers. It raises the pay to £14 an hour. What is the one thing that changed to bring in more workers?
steps.wrong: The number of care homes nearby
steps.hint: Nothing else about the job changed, only the money on offer.
steps.pre: That price paid for work is the

steps.q: At £9 an hour, 20 people were willing to work at the care home. At £14 an hour, 35 people are willing to work there. What is the 35 a measure of?
steps.right: How many workers are supplied at that wage
steps.wrong: How many patients the home can care for
steps.hint: Think about what number sits on the workers' side of this market at that wage.
steps.pre: That number of workers willing to work at a given wage is the

steps.q: As the wage rises from £9 to £14, the quantity of workers willing to work rises from 20 to 35. If wage is on the vertical axis and workers on the horizontal axis, does this line rise or fall as you move right?
steps.hint: Higher wage went with more workers, not fewer.
steps.pre: So wage and quantity of labour move together, giving an upward

steps.q: You already know how to plot a rising supply curve for a good like coffee, from low price/low quantity up to high price/high quantity. Can you use that same skill here, but with wage rate and workers instead of price and coffee?
steps.right: Yes, plot wage against quantity of workers the same way
